title: The Value of Being Metal-Poor
caption: The dwarf galaxy NGC 3109, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope
celestial: NGC 3109 · constellation Hydra · about 4 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: Dark Energy Survey/DOE/FNAL/DECam/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA. Image processing: R. Colombari & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: NGC 3109 shows blue hues in this view, but it is an irregular dwarf galaxy with no central bulge and no graceful spiral arms. It belongs to our Local Group of galaxies, lies around four million light-years away in the constellation Hydra, and measures about 40,000 light-years across.

It may look plain, but spectroscopic analysis shows that NGC 3109 ranks among the Local Group's most metal-poor galaxies. To astronomers, 'metals' means every element apart from hydrogen and helium, including carbon, nitrogen and oxygen. Stars forge these heavier elements from hydrogen and helium, then release them into space when they die, so later generations of stars contain them.

Because NGC 3109 has a composition similar to that of stars and galaxies in the early Universe, it may offer insight into how the chemistry of early galaxies evolved. The image was taken with the Dark Energy Camera on the NSF Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope in Chile.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (31.54 x 17.49 arcminutes) and distance (4 million light years), the frame spans roughly 37,000 × 20,000 light-years. Its light set out about 4 million years before reaching the telescope.
